newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--NYMEX heat even hotter after API stock drop.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--NYMEX heat even hotter after API stock drop.

text.p: Heat oil futures on the NYMEX got even hotter Tuesday evening after the American Petroleum Institute(API) released data showing distillate stocks failed to build and remain at their lowest levels in a generation.
The API said total distillate stocks fell last week by 17,000 barrels to 112.3 million -- 18.7 million below last year, amid views stocks would grow by one to two million.
Industry sources said they were much less interested in the API data showing a West Coast-led in drop crude stocks, and a rise in gasoline stocks fueled by poor demand.
Many sources said distillate exports to Europe were again the likely culprit behind U.S. refiners' failure to stock up voluminously on heating oil ahead of winter.
"The exports are a factor. If we didn't have the exports, we'd see a build of one or two million barrels," said Nizam Sharief, analyst at Houston-based Hornsby & Co.

While heating oil stocks on the East Coast, the largest heating oil market in the world, did rise by a slight 226,000 barrels to 23.7 million, sources said the build was too small to make a difference. They noted the industry is still playing a game of chicken with the prospect of winter price spikes.
"The fact that (East Coast) stocks rose by less than a million is a bit of a surprise and concern," Sharief said.

While sources agreed the API report could only make NYMEX heating oil prices go higher, some said prices on NYMEX's after-hours ACCESS system were going too high. The November heat contract was offered nearly a cent over its earlier settlement of 70.76 cents a gallon.
"ACCESS got a little excited, but when the dust settles overnight, it'll only be worth about 0.25 to 0.50 cent," said Jim Ritterbusch, a trader at Sweeney Oil Co in Chicago.
"I really don't see any surprises," he said of the report.

Crude stocks meanwhile fell by 6.1 million barrels to 302.3 million, according to the API report, but traders mostly dismissed the stock move since 3.2 million of it came from the West Coast, a market outside of the NYMEX orbit.
Equally unexciting were API's gasoline data showing total inventories rose by 2.2 million barrels to 197 million due in large part to declining demand typical of the autumn.

Indeed, November gasoline ignored the build and gained about 0.20 cent on ACCESS after settling at 62.82 cents a gallon, while November crude eked out a 20 cent gain after closing $24.14 a barrel during NYMEX's daytime session.
